source: Gittins (1979) Bandit processes and dynamic allocation indices (read via Wikipedia summary, not the paper)
finding: Gittins showed the optimal policy for independent bandit projects with discounted reward is an index policy: always play the project with the highest current index.
numbers: Index = sup over stopping times tau of expected discounted reward over expected discounted time, for discount beta<1. Weitzman reached the same result in economics in 1979.
quote: the Gittins index policy is optimal
limits: Only the secondary Wikipedia text was read, not the original paper. Needs independent arms, a known model per arm, geometric discounting, and only one arm evolving at a time.
agent_relevance: Gives the exact answer to which option gets the next sample when each option has a known prior. It is the ideal for G12-style allocation but needs a model per option.

source: Whittle (1980) Multi-armed bandits and the Gittins index (via Wikipedia)
finding: Whittle recast the index as a retirement problem: the index is the fixed payoff at which you are indifferent between continuing the arm and retiring.
numbers: w(i)=inf{k: v(i,k)=k}; nu(i)=(1-beta)*w(i).
limits: Secondary source only. Whittle also conjectured the index is a good heuristic for restless bandits; no optimality there.
agent_relevance: Retirement view maps onto a stop rule: keep sampling a branch while its value beats a sure fallback answer.

source: Weber (1992) On the Gittins index for multiarmed bandits, and computation methods (via Wikipedia)
finding: A short proof of the index theorem exists (Weber 1992). Exact algorithms compute indices: Varaiya 1985, Chen-Katehakis 1986, Katehakis-Veinott 1987, Sonin 2008, Nino-Mora 2007.
numbers: Restless bandits (arms evolve when not played) are in general NP-complete per the article; the index is only a heuristic there.
limits: Weber's paper itself was not opened; Wikipedia only lists the reference.
agent_relevance: Exact indices are cheap for small state spaces, so a Beta-Bernoulli model per branch could use them; the real limit is non-stationary, restless arms.

source: Wikipedia: Multi-armed bandit (history section)
finding: History: Robbins 1952 formulated the common modern version; Gittins 1979 gave the optimal discounted policy; Lai and Robbins 1985 built the fastest-converging policies; Burnetas and Katehakis 1996 widened the conditions.
numbers: Exp3 adversarial regret is O(sqrt(K T log K)). Epsilon-greedy typical epsilon 0.1.
limits: Secondary and partial: first 100000 of 124464 characters read. The page did not state the Lai-Robbins formula or UCB.
agent_relevance: Orientation only; the primary papers below carry the numbers.

source: Auer, Cesa-Bianchi, Fischer (2002) Finite-time analysis of the multiarmed bandit problem (Machine Learning 47)
finding: Lai and Robbins (1985) proved regret must grow at least logarithmically in plays. Auer et al. show simple index policies reach logarithmic regret uniformly over time, not just asymptotically.
numbers: Lai-Robbins: E[T_j(n)] <= (1/D(p_j||p*) + o(1)) ln n for each suboptimal arm j.
quote: regret for this problem has to grow at least logarithmically in the number of plays
limits: Bounded rewards in [0,1]. The Lai-Robbins constant is tight; the UCB1 constant is looser.
agent_relevance: A rule that samples a branch less than log-often cannot be sure it is not missing the best one; the price of certainty is log, not linear.

source: Auer et al. (2002) UCB1 theorem
finding: UCB1 plays the arm with highest (mean + sqrt(2 ln n / n_j)). Theorem 1 bounds expected regret after any n plays for any reward distribution on [0,1].
numbers: Regret <= sum over suboptimal arms of 8 ln n / Delta_i, plus (1 + pi^2/3) times the sum of the gaps. The leading 8/Delta^2 is worse than Lai-Robbins; the paper notes the factor 2 is the best possible when comparing 1/D to 1/(2 Delta^2).
limits: Bound is loose in the constant. The tuned variant UCB1-Tuned has no proved bound.
agent_relevance: A concrete optimism rule: add an exploration bonus that shrinks with the number of samples of that option. Cheap to implement over solution branches.

source: Auer et al. (2002) experiments: UCB1-Tuned, UCB2 and epsilon-greedy
finding: On Bernoulli bandits, UCB1-Tuned usually matched a well-tuned epsilon-greedy and was far less sensitive to tuning. Epsilon-greedy degrades fast if its parameter is off, and loses when many arms are clearly bad.
numbers: Seven distributions: 2 arms (0.9/0.6, 0.9/0.8, 0.55/0.45) and 10 arms (e.g. 0.9 then nine 0.6). 100,000 plays averaged over 100 runs. UCB2 alpha fixed at 0.001. UCB2 was always slightly worse than UCB1-Tuned.
limits: Simulation only with Bernoulli rewards. Tuned epsilon-greedy was best in most cases but needs per-problem tuning.
agent_relevance: Fixed-rate random exploration is fragile; confidence-based exploration is robust without per-task tuning.

source: Agrawal and Goyal (2012) Analysis of Thompson Sampling for the multi-armed bandit problem
finding: First proof that Thompson Sampling (1933) has logarithmic expected regret in the stochastic bandit. Sample each arm's mean from its posterior, play the arm with the largest sample.
numbers: Two arms: regret O(ln T / Delta + 1/Delta^3). N arms: O((sum_{i>=2} 1/Delta_i^2)^2 ln T). Optimal except for the Delta dependence and constants.
quote: for the first time, we show that Thompson Sampling algorithm achieves logarithmic expected regret
limits: Bernoulli rewards with Beta priors in the main proof. The N-arm bound is looser than UCB-style bounds.
agent_relevance: Probability matching spends samples in proportion to the chance a branch is best. Natural for a scaffold: pick a branch by its posterior win chance.

source: Russo, Van Roy, Kazerouni, Osband, Wen (2018) A tutorial on Thompson sampling
finding: Thompson sampling was proposed in 1933 and 1935 for clinical trials, largely ignored, rediscovered, and revived by Chapelle and Li (2011) and Scott (2010). It beats greedy and tuned epsilon-greedy in the paper's simulations.
numbers: Network routing example: each point is an average over 10,000 simulations; TS regret falls quickly, greedy does not. Applications listed: ads, A/B testing, revenue management, MCTS, recommenders.
limits: Tutorial; results come from simulations the authors set up. TS needs a posterior that can be sampled.
agent_relevance: Greedy exploitation of the current best branch fails; sampling from belief is a cheap fix.

source: Bubeck, Munos, Stoltz (2011) Pure exploration in finitely-armed and continuous-armed bandits (arXiv 0802.2655)
finding: When the goal is to find the best option, not to earn along the way, the right measure is simple regret. There is a trade-off: the better a strategy does on cumulative regret, the worse its simple regret.
numbers: Theorem 1: for K>=3 Bernoulli arms, any strategy with cumulative regret bounded by C f(n) has simple regret at least e^{-D f(n)} for some D, for some ordering. Cumulative-optimal play gives only polynomial decay of simple regret; uniform allocation gives exponential decay.
limits: Result is for Bernoulli arms and an unordered set of arms; some forecasters can get zero regret by luck on a given ordering.
agent_relevance: A scaffold that draws many attempts to pick a final answer is in the pure-exploration setting, so UCB-style focus on the leader is the wrong tool; spread samples then eliminate.

source: Garivier and Kaufmann (2016) Optimal best arm identification with fixed confidence (COLT)
finding: Gave the exact lower bound on samples needed to find the best arm with confidence 1-delta, and Track-and-Stop, an algorithm that matches it. It samples arms in the optimal proportions and stops with a Chernoff generalized-likelihood-ratio rule.
numbers: Table 1, delta=0.1, 3000 runs. Arms [0.5,0.45,0.43,0.4]: Track-and-Stop 3968 (BC) and 4052 (D-Tracking) draws, Chernoff-Racing 4516, KL-LUCB 8437, KL-Racing 9590. Arms [0.3,0.21,0.2,0.19,0.18]: 1370 / 1406 / 3078 / 2716 / 3334.
limits: One-parameter exponential families; optimal only asymptotically as delta goes to 0. Racing cannot reach the bound when the top two arms need unequal samples.
agent_relevance: Stop rules matter as much as sampling rules: the right stopping test halved the draws against a standard LUCB baseline in scenario 1.

source: Li, Jamieson, DeSalvo, Rostamizadeh, Talwalkar (2018) Hyperband (JMLR 18)
finding: Treats hyperparameter search as a pure-exploration infinite-armed bandit. Successive halving runs many configurations on a small budget, keeps the best 1/eta, and repeats. Hyperband runs several brackets to hedge the early-vs-late trade-off.
numbers: Over an order-of-magnitude speedup on CIFAR-10 and MRBI versus Bayesian optimisation; 5x faster than SMAC (early) on MRBI. Max theoretical speedup about 50x with linear training time; observed 6x to 70x versus random search. Overhead under 5%. On SVHN, SMAC (early) beat Hyperband.
limits: Assumes early performance predicts final performance. Bayesian methods were competitive on SVHN. Speedups depend on how training time scales with budget.
agent_relevance: Direct template for scaffold allocation: start many cheap attempts, cut losers early, spend on survivors. Works only if a cheap partial signal exists.

source: Hyperband: bracket structure and when early cutting fails
finding: Hyperband needs no prior on how fast configurations separate. Each bracket trades off number of configurations against budget per configuration; with R=81, eta=3 there are 5 brackets.
numbers: Most exploratory round evaluates R configurations at total budget (log_eta(R)+1)R.
limits: Early stopping can discard configurations that only pay off late (slow starters).
agent_relevance: Hedge: run a mix of aggressive and conservative cut rules rather than one fixed cut.

source: Krishnamurthy, Harris, Foster, Zhang, Slivkins (2024) Can large language models explore in-context? (NeurIPS 2024)
finding: GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama2 do not explore robustly in bandits when the history is in the prompt. Only one configuration worked: GPT-4 with a hint to explore, externally summarised per-arm averages, and chain of thought.
numbers: Hard instance K=5, gap 0.2; easy instance K=4, gap 0.5. 32 prompt designs for GPT-4 (T=100, N=10), GPT-3.5 over 48 configurations N=20 (about 200K queries); about 50K GPT-4 queries. Basic GPT-4 prompt, T=500, N=20: suffix failure in over 60% of replicates. Winning config, T=200, N=40: few suffix failures, reward close to Thompson Sampling.
quote: only one configuration resulted in satisfactory exploratory behavior
limits: Small bandits only. The same config without summarised history failed. Models are 2023 versions (GPT-4-0613, GPT-3.5-0613).
agent_relevance: Do not hand the model the raw log and hope it explores. Give it per-branch counts and means, and keep the allocation rule outside the model.

source: Krishnamurthy et al. (2024) failure modes: suffix failure and uniform failure
finding: Two failure modes: suffix failure (best arm never pulled again after some round, like Greedy) and uniform-like failure (all arms sampled equally, never narrows). Suffix failure at T=500 predicts poor long-run reward even when T=100 reward looks fine.
numbers: All but five GPT-4 configurations had suffix failure frequency of at least 15% at T/2. GPT-4 is much better than GPT-3.5; Llama2 is much worse, from Greedy-level to larger suffix failure. Behaviour was bimodal: some replicates lock onto the best arm fast, many rarely pull it.
limits: Surrogate statistics were designed because reward is too noisy at small T. Prompt changes interact, so no single fix was found.
agent_relevance: Track 'best branch never revisited' and 'all branches equal' as audit signals for the agent's own allocation.

source: Nie, Su, Chang, Lee, Chi, Le, Chen (2025) EVOLvE: Evaluating and optimizing LLMs for exploration (BanditBench)
finding: Benchmark of context-free and contextual bandits. Giving the LLM algorithm-guided support (UCB statistics computed outside) or distilling UCB trajectories by fine-tuning raises exploration; a fine-tuned Gemini-1.5 Flash beat Gemini-1.5 Pro.
numbers: Table 1 overall win rate, MAB: raw history Gemma-2B 7.6, Gemma-9B 10.5, Flash 27.7, Pro 45.5; summarised history Flash 34.8, Pro 60.0; algorithm-guided Flash 32.2, Pro 59.6; UCB 90.6. Contextual bandit: Flash raw 0.0, algorithm-guided Flash 46.4, Pro 64.3; LinUCB 96.4. 30 trials per configuration, t-test p<0.05.
limits: Fine-tuned model still below UCB (90.6 on MAB). Models are Gemma and Gemini 1.5 (2024).
agent_relevance: Even the best prompted model sits about 30 points below plain UCB. The scaffold should compute the allocation, not ask the model to feel it.

source: EVOLvE: oracle behaviour fine-tuning and few-shot demonstrations
finding: Fine-tuning on UCB trajectories helped most; few-shot demos helped the small model but hurt the large one. Hard-task demos helped fine-tuning but not few-shot.
numbers: Table 2 MAB win rate: few-shot raw history Flash 27.5, Pro 39.1; few-shot algorithm-guided Flash 50.2, Pro 56.4; fine-tuned algorithm-guided Flash 65.6. Few-shot on easy-task demos 50.2 vs hard 43.0; fine-tune on hard 65.6 vs easy 54.5. Fine-tune with raw history 28.3 in the context ablation.
limits: The paper's guess: manual few-shot examples disrupt the larger model's chain of thought. Some table cells were garbled in text extraction, so the row-to-cell mapping is my best reading.
agent_relevance: In-context demos can lower a strong model's allocation skill. Test any demo block against a no-demo control.

source: EVOLvE: regret scaling by model size
finding: Fitting regret curves, stronger models (Gemini-1.5 Pro) show sublinear regret growth; weaker Gemma-2B and 9B stay on a linear regret path, so they do not learn which arm is best.
numbers: Parametric fit with a log term for sublinear growth and a linear term for failure to match the optimal algorithm.
limits: The fit is empirical, not a proof.
agent_relevance: Small models cannot be trusted to self-allocate; use external rules for them.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (PNAS), horizon task
finding: On a two-armed bandit (Wilson horizon task), GPT-3 had lower regret than humans overall, but showed no sign of directed exploration and ignored the horizon.
numbers: GPT-3 mean regret 2.72 (SD 5.98) vs humans 3.24 (SD 10.26), t(38878) = -5.03, p<.001. Short horizon: no difference from humans (t(5566) = -0.043). Horizon x reward-difference interaction beta=-0.02+/-0.02, p=.14, so no strategic random exploration; no directed exploration.
limits: GPT-3 (text-davinci) from 2022. Humans improved more within a task and ended with slightly lower final regret (not significant).
agent_relevance: A model can look good on regret by exploiting while not exploring on purpose; it does not use the horizon unless told and made to act on it.

source: Coda-Forno, Binz, Akata, Botvinick, Wang, Schulz (2023) Meta-in-context learning in LLMs
finding: GPT-3 learns within a two-armed bandit (regret falls over about 4 trials, then flat) and gets better across tasks when earlier tasks stay in the prompt. It matches Greedy after four tasks and lags UCB slightly.
numbers: 500 simulations. In-context effect beta=-0.221+/-0.012, t=-35.828, p<.001; meta-in-context effect beta=-0.031+/-0.012, t=-5.002, p<.001.
limits: Small two-armed task; old GPT-3 models. The across-task gain is small compared with the within-task effect.
agent_relevance: Past solved problems in context can sharpen allocation, but gains are small; do not count on them.

source: Park, Liu, Ozdaglar, Zhang (2025) Do LLM agents have regret? (arXiv 2403.16843)
finding: Pretrained LLMs often reach sublinear regret in online learning with full feedback and in stochastic bandits. But GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo fail on simple adversarial sequences; a trained regret-loss fixes it.
numbers: Horizons T=100, 200 and 500 tested (GPT-4o still sublinear at T=500). Failure cases: alternating loss sequence and noisy alternating sequence; 20 repeated runs; linear regret could not be rejected for GPT-4 and GPT-4 Turbo. A regret-loss transformer reached sublinear regret.
limits: Failures are on constructed adversarial counterexamples (Hazan 2016, Feder et al. 1992), not natural tasks. GPT-3.5 was worse than GPT-4.
agent_relevance: LLM allocation may look fine on stationary tasks and still break on shifting or adversarial signals.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large language monkeys: scaling inference compute with repeated sampling
finding: Coverage (fraction solved by at least one of k samples) grows near log-linearly over orders of magnitude, so many cheap samples can lift weak models, but only when a verifier can pick the right one.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250. CodeContests, Gemma-2B: 0.02% with 1 sample to 7.1% with 10,000 (over 300x). MATH, Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000, but majority vote or reward model only 40.50% to 41.41%.
limits: Gains need an automatic verifier. Majority voting and reward models did not close the coverage gap.
agent_relevance: Many samples are worth spending only if the final choice is checked by something external (tests, a verifier).

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally (arXiv 2408.03314)
finding: The best way to spend test-time compute depends on prompt difficulty. A per-prompt compute-optimal strategy beats best-of-N using about 4x less compute, and in a FLOPs-matched test beat a 14x larger model on problems where the small model has non-trivial success.
numbers: Difficulty in 5 bins by the model's own pass@1 over 2048 samples. Easy (levels 1-2): beam search got worse as budget rose (verifier exploited). Hard (levels 3-4): beam search beat best-of-N. Level 5: no method made meaningful progress.
limits: MATH benchmark, PaLM 2 models; difficulty estimated from the model's own samples. On hard questions or high inference load, scaling pretraining was better than test-time compute.
agent_relevance: Spend by difficulty and not on hopeless prompts: this is the empirical basis for G12.

source: Damani, Shenfeld, Peng, Bobu, Andreas (2024) Learning how hard to think: input-adaptive allocation of LM computation
finding: Predict the reward distribution per query and budget, then give more samples to queries where extra compute helps most (greedy allocation, a matroid). Matches fixed-budget quality with up to 50% less compute (code) or up to 10% higher quality at fixed budget.
numbers: Code: same performance with up to 50% less compute; Chat: matches reward with up to 10% less; routing saves 25-40% of calls to the expensive model. About 50% of coding problems have zero success probability (Math 5%). Difficulty-predictor accuracy reported 72% to 84% in the table I read.
limits: Needs a trained difficulty predictor; zero-success problems tempt the allocator to waste budget (a predicted 1% success becomes an attractive bet).
agent_relevance: Cap spending on problems with no foothold. Use a cheap difficulty probe before big sampling.

source: Synthesis: Gittins vs UCB vs Thompson vs successive halving for scaffold allocation
finding: Four families fit different goals. Gittins: exact optimum with known priors and discounting. UCB and Thompson: low cumulative regret when each pull also earns. Best-arm identification, successive halving and Hyperband: pure exploration, as in picking a final answer.
numbers: Cumulative-regret optimal rules give simple regret only polynomial decay (Bubeck 2011); uniform sampling gives exponential. Track-and-Stop needs 3968 draws vs 8437 for KL-LUCB on a 4-arm instance (Garivier-Kaufmann).
limits: This line is my reading across the opened papers, not a single source's result.
agent_relevance: Choose the family by goal. In a scaffold, final answer quality is a pure-exploration goal, so use halving or best-arm rules.

source: Evidence gap note: primary Gittins, Lai-Robbins, Thompson papers not opened
finding: Original Gittins (1979), Lai-Robbins (1985), Robbins (1952), Thompson (1933) and Weber (1992) were not read in full. Facts about them come from Auer et al. (2002), Russo et al. (2018) and Wikipedia.
numbers: Web search quota was exhausted; Semantic Scholar returned 429; the arXiv API returned 429 or nothing.
limits: Treat their lines as second-hand.
agent_relevance: Re-check against the originals before citing exact constants.
